items.summary: Ayurveda sees fever as weakened digestion (agnimandya) producing toxins (ama) that spread through the body. Treatment begins with fasting or light food to "digest" the ama, then bitter herbs.
items.types: Eight types: Vataja, Pittaja, Kaphaja, three dual-dosha types, Sannipatika (all three) and Agantuja (external causes). Formulations are chosen by stage: Sama (with ama, first ~7 days) or Nirama.

Confusion, drowsiness, fits
Bleeding (gums, nose, rash of tiny spots), possible dengue
Severe vomiting, no urine, signs of dehydration
Stiff neck, difficulty breathing
Fever lasting more than 3 days, or after travel to a malaria area

evidence.label: Very limited evidence
evidence.clinical: There are no good-quality trials for Ayurvedic fever treatment. Fever is a symptom: the cause (malaria, dengue, typhoid, pneumonia, urinary infection) must be identified.
evidence.traditional: Classical textual description; not equivalent to clinical-trial evidence.

items.standardCare: Get tested for the cause, especially after travel or in the rainy season. Use paracetamol and fluids; antibiotics or antimalarials when an infection is confirmed. Do not rely on herbs for suspected dengue, malaria or bacterial infection.
items.guidelineNote: Level 3, fever-specific: dengue, Kalingadi Kashaya 20–40 ml twice daily for 5–7 days; malaria, Sudarshana Ghana Vati 1–3 tablets; influenza, Sudarshana Churna 2–4 g.

yoga.caution: Rest during fever; resume yoga only after recovery.

items.summary: Grahani is the part of the gut that holds food until it is digested. When digestive fire weakens, food passes undigested or held back, giving alternating loose and hard stools. Charaka calls buttermilk the best remedy.
items.types: Vataja, Pittaja, Kaphaja and Sannipataja Grahani; Sangrahagrahani (with mucus and cramps). Treat as for Ajirna and Atisara, with Langhana, Pachana and Deepana.
symptoms: Urgency after meals, mucus in stools
Bloating, wind, cramping relieved by passing stool
redFlags: Blood in stools

Waking at night with diarrhoea

items.summary: White patches of skin, described by Charaka at the end of the skin-disease chapter as hard to cure. Bakuchi seed, its main classical remedy, is the origin of the psoralen used in modern PUVA light therapy.

redFlags: Rapid spread
Signs of thyroid disease (tiredness, weight change)
White patches with numbness (rule out leprosy)

items.summary: Autism is not described in any classical text; it was first named in the 1940s. Modern Ayurveda paediatric (Kaumarabhritya) departments manage it under Unmada (mental disorders) and childhood developmental conditions.
items.types: Approaches reported by government Ayurveda hospitals: medhya (intellect-promoting) ghritas such as Brahmi, Kalyanaka and Saraswata ghrita (an AIIA trial uses Shankhapushpi with Saraswata ghrita); Pratimarsha Nasya with Anu taila; Shirodhara; Shiro Basti; Abhyanga. Doses are weight-based and set by the specialist, so none are listed here.
symptoms: Difficulty with social communication and eye contact
redFlags: Loss of speech or skills the child already had
Seizures
Self-injury or not eating
Any developmental concern: get assessed early; early therapy changes outcomes
pathya: Regular routine for meals and sleep
Fresh, simple food
Calm, predictable environment
apathya: Rasa (metal-containing) medicines
Vacha (calamus) in children
Chelation or "detox" claims: dangerous for children
items.course: Only under a paediatric Ayurveda specialist, alongside developmental therapies.

evidence.label: Very limited evidence

items.standardCare: Early intervention has the strongest evidence: speech therapy, occupational therapy and behavioural or developmental therapy (ABA, Early Start Denver Model). Ayurveda, if used, should be an add-on, never a replacement.
